qIntro: Legal decisions mean you have the authority to make decisions for your children in things like medical matters, school decisions, and extracurricular activities.
qText: Do you and your co-parent want to make legal decisions for your children together, or should only one parent be allowed to make these decisions?

Unless you agree otherwise, both you and your co-parent have:
i.	The right to participate in major decisions about your child’s heath, social situations, morals, welfare, education and economic development.
ii.	The right to talk to your child on the phone when they are with their other parent.
iii.	The right to participate in choosing doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists, hospitals, and other health care providers for your child.
iv.	The right to authorize medical, surgical, hospital, dental, institutional, psychological, and psychiatric care for your child and to get a second opinion about their medical conditions or treatment.
v.	The right to be told about if your child gets sick or injured.
vi.	The right to attend your child’s medical, dental, and other-health related appointments and treatments.
vii.	The right to get and inspect your child’s medical and dental records and the right to talk to any treating physician, dentist, and other health care provider.
viii.	The right to talk with schools officials about your child’s welfare and educational status, and the right to get and inspect your child’s school records to the extent permitted by law.
ix.	The right together copies of all school reports, calendars of schools events, notices of parent-teacher conferences, and school programs.
x.	The right to attend and participate in parent-teach conferences, school trips, school programs, and other school activities that parents are invited to.
xi.	The right to attend and participate with your children in athletic programs and other extracurricular activities.
xii.	The right to get notice of the other parent’s intention to move.

Next, you will build a parenting time schedule that shows when you and your co-parent will each spend time with your children. This schedule will cover weekdays, weekends, holidays, special occasions, and vacations.
i.	You and your co-parent will decide on a set schedule for when your child will stay with each of you, and this plan includes regular school days, weekends, holidays, and summer vacations. Once your judge approves this plan, both of you must follow this schedule.
ii.	If both you and your co-parent agree, you can choose to change the schedule on your own. However, if one parents stops following the new plan, the Court cannot help or step in unless a judge has officially signed off on the change.
iii.	During your parenting time with your child, you should support a positive relationship between your children and your co-parent. This means that you shouldn’t do anything that may damage their relationship or cause your child to think less of their other parent. Your co-parent should do the same.
iv.	Both parents should be careful when planning appointments or fun events. You should not pick times that are meant to annoy the other parent or make their life difficult. It is important to remember that kids need to enjoy their activities without any drama. Both parents should support the children and let them go to their activities without a struggle.

qText: If your child gets a serious injury, stays sick for a long time, or has to go to the emergency room or hospital, you need to tell the other parent right away. You should tell them what happened, how the child is doing, and where the child is. You need to share the information as soon as possible and definitely within 24 hours of the emergency. Additionally, both parents must give each other the names and phone numbers for all of the doctors and healthcare workers who take care of the child.

If the parent who is the “residential parent” plans to move to a new home that is not the one listed in the parenting plan, that parent must tell the Court before moving. After the Court gets the notice, it will send a notice to the “non‑residential parent.” The Court or the non‑residential parent may then ask for a hearing. Both parents will be told about the hearing. The hearing is to decide if any changes should be made to the parenting plan to make sure the child’s best interests are protected.

The non-residential parent has the same legal right to see all of the child or children’s records, just as the residential parent does, unless the Court has placed limits on that access. Anyone who keeps these records must follow the Court’s orders about sharing them. If they do not follow the orders, they could face legal penalties.
Relevant Ohio Statute can be found here: R.C. 3109.051(H), 3319.321(B)(5)(a), R.C. 3125.16 and 3319.321(F)

Both parents have the right to visit the child’s daycare. This is determined by law under Ohio Revised Code § 5104.039. Even if the child does not live with you most of the time, you can go to the daycare center just like the other parent can. However, this is subject to other agreements between parents, or a specific court order that says you are not allowed to.

Both parents are allowed to go to their child’s school activities. If one parent is allowed to go to a school event (like a game or a play), the other parent is allowed to go too. They must follow the same rules as everyone else. If a school worker tries to stop a parent from coming in person, they could get in trouble with the court (something called contempt). The only time this changes is if there is an agreement between parents or if the judge makes a special rule to stop a parent from attending.

qText:
i.	If you are the parent who must provide health insurance for the child(ren), you have to give the other parent the following within 30 days after this support order is issued:
	1.	Information about the benefits, limitations, and exclusions of the health plan.
	2.	Copies of forms needed to get money back for medical costs.
	3.	Payments or other benefits of the insurance.
	4.	Proof of insurance that shows the child(ren) are covered.
ii.	Within thirty (30) days after the order is given, the person who is providing health care for the child(ren) must send proof of the of that healthcare to the Child Support Enforcement Agency.
iii.	The person who must provide healthcare to the child or children must list that child or children as dependent(s) on any healthcare plan they have.
iv.	The employer of the person providing healthcare to the child or children must give certain healthcare information to the other parent, anyone included in a court order, or the Child Support Enforcement Agency. This information may include the name and address of the health plan administrator and the policy or plan number.
	Relevant Ohio Statute can be found here: R.C. 3119.32(E), R.C. 3109.19 & R.C. 3119.31

v.	If the person who must provide health care for the child or children gets a new job, the Child Support Enforcement Agency may send the new employer a notice telling them to enroll the child or children into the health care coverage offered at the new job if no other insurance is in place.
	Relevant Ohio Statute can be found here: R.C. 3119.32(G) & R.C.3119.34

You have decided to defer to your co-parent.

If your co-parent is the one who will list your child on their taxes this year, you must give them a specific form called IRS Form 8332. ii.	If you wrote down that you are NOT the residential parent earlier on this form, your co-parent has a job to do.
